question: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with his family because of abdominal pain, excessive urination and drowsiness since the day before. He has had type 1 diabetes mellitus for 2 years. He ran out of insulin 2 days ago. His vital signs at admission include a temperature of 36.8°C (98.24°F), a blood pressure of 102/69 mmHg, and a pulse of 121/min. On physical examination, he is lethargic and his breathing is rapid and deep. There is a mild generalized abdominal tenderness without rebound tenderness or guarding. His serum glucose is 480 mg/dL. The patient is admitted to the intensive care unit and management is started. Which of the following is considered a resolution criterion for this patient's condition?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Insulin deficiency" -> "Hyperglycemia" -> "Ketoacidosis" -> "Increased serum acetone" -> "Disappearance of serum acetone" -> 70% CHAIN: "Insulin deficiency" -> "Hyperglycemia" -> "Ketoacidosis" -> "Metabolic acidosis" -> "Anion gap < 10" -> 80% CHAIN: "Insulin deficiency" -> "Hyperglycemia" -> "Ketoacidosis" -> "Metabolic acidosis" -> "Bicarbonate < 10 mEq/L" -> 70%
enhanced_information: In a patient with type 1 diabetes mellitus presenting with hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis due to insulin deficiency, the resolution criterion for his condition would be the disappearance of serum acetone. This is because as the ketoacidosis resolves with appropriate treatment, the serum acetone levels decrease. Anion gap < 10 and bicarbonate < 10 mEq/L are indicators of metabolic acidosis, which is a part of the pathophysiology but not a direct resolution criterion. Hyperkalemia and increased blood urea nitrogen are complications associated with diabetic ketoacidosis but not resolution criteria.
analysis: In a patient with type 1 diabetes mellitus presenting with hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis due to insulin deficiency, the resolution criterion for his condition is the disappearance of serum acetone.
